study.title: Joshua 2 - The faith of Rahab and the encouragement of the spies
study.overview: Joshua sends two men to observe Jericho before the crossing of the Jordan, and the narrative revolves around a strong contrast: the king of Jericho reacts with fear and control, while Rahab reacts with fear of the LORD and faith in his works. She protects the spies, recognizes that the God of Israel is sovereign over heaven and earth, asks for mercy for his family and receives a sign of security. The chapter ends with the return of the spies to Joshua and with the confirmation that the land was already psychologically shaken before Israel. The text highlights both human prudence and God's action, which prepares the conquest even before the conflict begins.

outline.title: The Secret Mission and Protection of Raabe
outline.explanation: Joshua sends two spies to Jericho. They enter the house of Rahab, and the king learns of their presence. Rahab hides men and diverts the king's agents, allowing them to escape. The scene shows real risk, practical discernment and Raabe's house as an unexpected sheltering place.

outline.title: The confession of faith of Rahab and the agreement of mercy
outline.explanation: Before the spies utter, Rahab declares that he knows that the LORD gave the land to Israel. She interprets the deeds of God in the exodus and in the victories over the Amorites as proof that the Lord is God above in the heavens and below on earth. In response, she asks for preservation for her family, and the spies promise mercy, provided she does not denounce them.

outline.title: The escape through the window and the sign of the scarlet cord
outline.explanation: Rahab descends the spies by a rope, guides them to hide for three days and receives clear instructions: gather the family at home and tie a scarlet cord in the window. The sign links the promise to obedience and sets the limits of the responsibility of the spies and the protected house.

outline.title: The return of the spies and the confirmation of the fear of the residents
outline.explanation: The spies remain hidden until the persecutors give up, return to Joshua and report everything. The final report confirms that the Lord has already delivered the land into his hands and that the inhabitants are terrified. The chapter ends by strengthening Israel's confidence before the entry into Jericho.

study.context: The chapter presupposes Israel encamped in Sitim, on the east side of the Jordan, before Jericho. Joshua sends spies to observe the city on the immediate route of entry into Canaan. The notes indicate that Jericho needed to be examined carefully because of his strategic position and defenses. The text also suggests a scenario in which news of Israel's victories over peoples to the east of the Jordan had already spread, producing panic among the inhabitants of the land.
study.theology: Joshua 2 presents several central theological themes. First, the sovereignty of the LORD: it is not only Israel that moves, but God who is already delivering the land. Second, faith is born from listening to the acts of God: Rahab interprets the exodus and previous victories as evidence of divine power and responds with reverent fear. Third, mercy and covenant unite: Rahab's house is preserved not by ethnic merit, but by the confidence shown and the commitment made. Fourth, the chapter shows that God can use a person outside the people of Israel to confess the truth about him and serve the advancement of his purposes. As for Rahab's lie, the text narrates it without explicit approval; confessional readings can assess their act differently, but the main focus of the passage falls on their faith, their protection to the spies and the faithfulness of God in fulfilling the promise.

scholarViews.insight: The note highlights that Joshua sent the spies strategically because Jericho was the unavoidable entry point for Israel upon arriving in Canaan.
The comment notes that Rahab encourages the spies by recognizing what God has already done and by informing the panic that dominated Jericho, strengthening Israel's trust.
The note explains that the final report of the spies strongly contrasts with human fear: they claim that the Lord has already delivered the land and that the residents were taken in fear.

questions: What does Joshua's decision to send spies teaches about prudence without unbelief, especially when God has already promised the land?
Why is Rahab's confession to the LORD so important in the chapter, and what does it reveal about true faith?
How do the promise made to the spies and the sign of the scarlet cord show that God's mercy is received with confidence and obedience?
study.practice: Read this chapter as an invitation to practical trust. When God has spoken, it is still wise to act responsibly, as Joshua did. When the situation seems dominated by fear, remember that the Lord may be preparing people and circumstances even before you even see the outcome. Apply this in a concrete way: pray before difficult decisions, act with discernment and seek to be someone who, like Rahab, recognizes the truth about God and responds with courage. Also examine your home and your relationships: is there room to welcome, protect and act responsibly?
study.uncertainty: The scores provided do not definitively resolve the moral assessment of Rahab's lie; they only record the fact of the report and, in a comment, recognize the issue. There is also a textual observation in Adam Clarke about the position of Joshua 2:15 within the narrative, but this does not alter the main reading of the chapter. It is not possible to affirm, only with these notes, additional historical details about Sitim beyond what was mentioned, nor to identify with absolute certainty the exact nature of Raabe's house (hostage, prostitution or both) without leaving the material given.
